Many objectives find a common formalization in the expected free energy (EFE) framework of active inference 1. EFE can be decomposed into two terms: (i) risk–the KL divergence between predicted and preferred outcomes, capturing the expected cost of a policy relative to homeostatic, rewarding, and normative goals–and (ii) ambiguity–the expected entropy of observations given hidden states, capturing uncertainty in the mapping from (belief) states to outcomes 2. By selecting policies that minimize EFE, agents automatically balance exploitation and exploration. Mathematically, for a policy π\pi, EFE is: A 2026 active-inference model simulates belief updating (Figure) 3. The authors test information gain in policy selection (Figure).

G(π)=DKL[Q(oτ|π)∥P(oτ)]⏟risk (expected cost)+𝔼Q(oτ,sτ|π)[H[P(oτ|sτ)]]⏟ambiguity\begin{equation} G(\pi) = \underbrace{D_{KL}[Q(o_\tau|\pi) \| P(o_\tau)]}_{\text{risk (expected cost)}} + \underbrace{\mathbb{E}_{Q(o_\tau, s_\tau|\pi)}[H[P(o_\tau|s_\tau)]]}_{\text{ambiguity}} \end{equation}

This equation makes the brain’s "objective" look like preference satisfaction + uncertainty reduction, expressed in a single control functional. The first term (risk) says: choose policies whose predicted future outcomes (Q(oτ|π)Q(o_\tau|\pi)) look like the outcomes the organism "wants" to encounter, where "want" is encoded as a prior preference distribution P(oτ)P(o_\tau). In active inference, that preference distribution is where homeostatic setpoints, learned rewards, and social/normative goals all live–so value is not a separate add-on, but a prior over outcomes that action tries to realize. Concretely, minimizing DKL[Q(oτ|π)||P(oτ)]D_{KL}[Q(o_\tau|\pi)||P(o_\tau)] is equivalent to minimizing expected "cost" (negative log preference). The second term (ambiguity) says: choose policies that visit states where the likelihood mapping P(oτ|sτ)P(o_\tau|s_\tau) is sharp (low-entropy)–i.e. where we know what observation(s) to expect when entering a given state. This term formalizes an epistemic drive: actions that reduce ambiguity are actions that (on average) improve state-estimation and world-model accuracy, yielding the explore/exploit tradeoff without bolting on a separate "curiosity bonus."

Both terms emerge from a single variational principle–minimizing EFE is equivalent to maximizing model evidence (minimizing long-run surprise), so the framework inherits the mathematical rigor of variational Bayesian inference. The decomposition isn’t arbitrary: risk and ambiguity naturally separate when expanding the expected log probability of preferred outcomes, reflecting the fundamental distinction between getting what you want and knowing what’s going on. Importantly, EFE subsumes standard RL–under certain conditions (known dynamics, flat priors except for reward), EFE minimization reduces to expected reward maximization–making it a generalization that explains when reward-based models succeed and why they fail for information-seeking behaviors with no instrumental payoff.

This formalization is important because it provides a single objective that (a) makes value precise as a prior over outcomes (so homeostasis, learned reward, and norms can live in one place), and (b) makes curiosity/epistemic action a first-class consequence of optimal control rather than a bolt-on bonus. That unification matters for brain theory: it explains why organisms routinely take actions that look "non-reward-maximizing" in the short term (checking, sampling, exploring, seeking clarity) while still serving long-run viability and goal attainment–because reducing ambiguity is instrumentally valuable for keeping the world-model calibrated and control stable.

Evolution "bakes in" both EFE terms by shaping (a) what outcomes count as acceptable and (b) how much the organism should pay to be less wrong about hidden state before committing to action. The risk term is installed by hard-wiring a preference landscape over outcomes: there are steep fitness cliffs (hypoxia, hypoglycemia, dehydration, hyperthermia, injury, social expulsion) where small prediction errors can become irreversible. Brains that treat predicted proximity to those cliffs as intrinsically costly outcompete brains that don’t. Mechanistically, this shows up as deep "viability priors" implemented via interoceptive control loops (brainstem/hypothalamus/insula), threat and aversive-learning circuits (amygdala-PAG, extended amygdala, habenula), and basal ganglia gating that biases policy selection away from outcome distributions historically correlated with loss of viability. In EFE language, selection tunes P(oτ)P(o_\tau) (preferred outcomes) to concentrate probability mass on states compatible with survival/reproduction, so minimizing DKL[Q(oτ|π)∥P(oτ)]D_{KL}[Q(o_\tau|\pi) \| P(o_\tau)] becomes a generic way to avoid low-fitness regions of outcome space.

The ambiguity term is installed because, for embodied agents, control is only as good as state estimation: actions chosen under a misidentified state can be catastrophically wrong (eat the wrong berry; approach the wrong silhouette; misread dominance cues). So evolution favors architectures that treat expected identifiability of the world as a first-class control variable. This yields brains built as hierarchical generative models whose default operation is to reduce prediction error via precision-weighted inference, plus a set of active-sensing "moves" (orienting reflexes, saccades, sniffing/whisking, head turns, information-seeking locomotion) that deliberately place the organism in states where the likelihood mapping is sharper.

Neuromodulators serve the ambiguity term by (i) tuning precision weights (gain) on prediction-error pathways so the brain trusts the right evidence at the right level, (ii) gating plasticity to learn a sharper P(o|s)P(o|s), and (iii) modulating policy precision and exploration regimes so the agent chooses actions that land it in states with more diagnostic observations. Evolution makes this possible with a very specific control architecture: a handful of small, phylogenetically old "hub" nuclei (brainstem/basal forebrain/midbrain) that (a) integrate high-level summary signals about surprise, arousal, interoceptive state, and action outcomes, then (b) broadcast slow control signals via massively branching, diffuse projections across cortex-thalamus-hippocampus-basal ganglia, using receptor families that are heterogeneously expressed by layer/cell-type/synapse so the same chemical broadcast can selectively change gain, learning rate, and gating in the right microcircuits.
